KEY MESSAGE 1...

A 1040 mb area of high pressure positioned across the Northeast
today will provide dry conditions along with seasonably cool 
temperatures for any pre-holiday travel today. Despite increasing
clouds today ahead of our incoming storm, the cirrus canopy will
still support radiational cooling resulting in another chilly 
night. Expect early Thanksgiving temperatures to drop into the 
upper teens to upper 20s.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

Latest water vapor imagery shows a robust area of convection 
developing off the coast of Florida. This is a result of strong
diffluent flow ahead of a southern stream shortwave trough that
is taking on a negative tilt through the Gulf Coast states.
Continued strong forcing for ascent will allow our coastal 
storm to develop and deepen this evening and track up the East 
coast. The strong pressure gradient between the storm and the 
1040hPa high to its north will allow a very intense east-
southeast low-level jet to form ahead of it with the u-component
of the winds ranking on the extreme end of the NAEFS model 
climatology. This is quite notable and will result in a very 
robust moisture fetch that also ranks among the NAEFS all-time 
highest values in the model climatology extending from the 
tropics northward. As the southern stream shortwave phases with
the parent closed low to its west, our coastal storm will be 
steered further inland early Thursday and track up the spine of 
the Appalachian mountains. 

While the storm will weaken some, the powerhouse low-level jet 
and rich moisture plume will remain steadfast with impressive 
isentropic lift supporting an organized leading band of moderate
to heavy rain. Latest high resolution guidance continues to 
show the large scale ridging over the Northeast delaying the 
south to north advancing rain shield until Thursday afternoon 
giving a dry Thanksgiving morning. Rain will fall moderate to 
heavily as it pushes into areas south of I-90 between 18 - 21 
UTC and areas along and north of I-90 by 21 - 03 UTC. Hourly 
rainfall rates 0.10 - 0.25 inches can result in poor drainage 
and urbanized flooding but the dry antecedent conditions should
mitigate widespread flooding concerns. The strong easterly 
winds will also result in enhanced rainfall rates along the east
facing slopes of the southern Greens, southern Adirondacks, and
northern/eastern Catskills. The heaviest rainfall rates will 
last through Thursday evening which can result in reduced 
visibility and slow travel for those returning home from 
Thanksgiving activities. Luckily, the dry slot races northward 
as the sfc low becomes absorbed into the parent cyclone, 
bringing an end to the heavy rainfall rates near or shortly 
after Midnight with just lingering scattered showers overnight. 
Total rainfall amounts still range between 0.75 and 1.50 inches 
with the NBM probabilistic guidance highlighting the east facing
slopes of the southern Adirondacks, eastern Catskills, and 
southern Greens with greater than 75% chance of exceeding 1.50 
inches. There is even a 40 to 60% chance of exceeding 2 inches 
in the eastern Catskills due to upslope flow. Areas west of the 
Taconics will likely see lower amounts due to downsloping. The
Hudson River at Poughkeepsie looks to also result in minor 
flooding during the Thursday early afternoon high tide cycle.

Besides the heavy rain, areas at and above 1500ft in elevation
in the southern Adirondacks, eastern Catskills and southern 
Greens will likely start off as freezing rain late Thursday
afternoon into the evening as very low dew points and dry air in
the low-level at the onset supporting wet-bulb cooling 
processes as the warm nose aloft intensifies. Given increased 
confidence in freezing rain resulting in slippery travel, we 
issued a Winter Weather Advisory from 21 UTC Thurs to 12 UTC Fri
for these areas. Warming temperatures overnight should allow 
freezing rain to transition to plain rain by early Friday.

KEY MESSAGE 3...

Our powerhouse easterly jet in the low and mid-levels continues
to raise concerns of gusty winds developing ahead of and during
our incoming storm tomorrow afternoon into the evening hours.
While forecast soundings showing an intense 60 to 80kt jet in 
the 850 - 700hPa layer, there is a notable inversion thanks to
the incoming warm sector which will mitigate the core of these
strong winds from mixing the surface. However, winds at the top
of the mixed layer reach near 40-50kts and the incoming marine
modified air mass should help reduce stability in the low- 
levels. Thus, the momentum transfer combined with downsloping
effect should result in the strongest gusts in western New 
England, the Taconics, and eastern Catskills reaching up to 40 
to 50kts. Channeled flow down the Mohawk Valley should also 
enhance wind gusts in the western Mohawk Valley. The latest NBM 
probabilistic guidance shows low spread between the 25th and
75th percentile for the max wind gusts in the 24hr window ending
1AM Fri
